lead: A rectifier gives pulsating DC: the voltage swings from zero up to the peak and back, at twice the supply frequency in a full-wave circuit. A capacitor across the load stores charge at the peak and returns it in the gaps. An inductor in series blocks fast current changes. Together they make a nearly steady DC. Phone chargers and inverter DC links use this.
prereq: You need 2.1 for the unsmoothed output waveform.

blocks.text: Only a few universities teach this chapter; most stop at the raw rectified waveform.

Connect a capacitor C across the load. While the rectified voltage climbs to its peak Vm, the diodes conduct and charge C almost to Vm. When the rectified voltage falls below the capacitor voltage, every diode is reverse biased and C alone feeds the load, discharging through R with time constant RC. The output becomes a small sawtooth sitting near Vm.
Vr = Idc / (2fC)  (full wave)      Vr = Idc / (fC)  (half wave)
blocks.where: Vr is the peak-to-peak ripple in V, Idc the load DC current in A, f the supply frequency in Hz, C the capacitance in F. Assumes RC much greater than 1/f, small ripple and ideal diodes.
Vm is the peak of the rectified waveform in V. The average sits midway between the peak and the trough.

blocks.text: Ripple grows with load current, so a capacitor filter suits light loads: holding the same ripple at 10 A needs ten times the capacitance of 1 A. The diode conducts only near the peak, so the same charge arrives in short tall pulses and the repetitive peak diode current can be several times Idc. In a full-wave circuit the peak inverse voltage is unchanged by the capacitor (Vm per diode in a bridge, 2Vm in a centre-tap circuit). In a half-wave circuit the capacitor raises it from Vm to 2Vm, because the diode must block the capacitor voltage plus the reverse supply peak.

An inductor in series with the load opposes change of current. It stores energy when the rectified voltage is above the load voltage and gives it back in the dips. The ripple current falls roughly in proportion to 1/(2πf_r L), where f_r is the ripple frequency (2f for full wave, f for half wave) and L is in henries. Doubling the reactance — double L, or double f_r — halves the ripple current. A series inductor works better at heavy load, where the current stays continuous.

The L-C filter puts L in series and C across the load. L blocks the ripple current, C absorbs what is left. The output ripple falls to roughly 1/((2πf_r)²LC) of the ripple entering the filter; for example, LC = 0.01 s² at f_r = 100 Hz gives about 1/4 of the input ripple.
A bleeder resistor across C draws a small fixed current. It keeps the inductor working at light load and discharges C after switch-off.

figure.caption: Full-wave, 100 Hz ripple, 2 A load, f = 50 Hz: 1000 µF gives 20 V peak-to-peak, and doubling the capacitor halves the ripple, so cutting ripple by ten needs ten times the capacitance.

spec.aria: A curve falling steeply and then flattening, showing ripple voltage against filter capacitance from 500 microfarads to 2000 microfarads, for a 2 A load, full wave at 50 Hz.

examples.question: A bridge rectifier works from a 230 V, 50 Hz supply and feeds a load drawing Idc = 2 A through a 1000 µF filter capacitor. Estimate the ripple voltage and the DC output voltage.
steps: Peak of the rectified waveform: Vm = 230 × √2 = 325.27 V.
Ripple, full wave: Vr = Idc/(2fC) = 2 / (2 × 50 × 1000 × 10⁻⁶) = 20 V.
The average sits half a ripple below the peak: Vdc ≈ Vm − Vr/2 = 325.27 − 10 = 315.27 V.
Check: R = Vdc/Idc = 157.6 Ω, so RC = 0.158 s, about eight cycles of 20 ms. The linear-discharge approximation is fair.
examples.answer: Ripple Vr ≈ 20 V peak-to-peak and DC output Vdc ≈ 315.3 V.
examples.check:
import math
Vrms = 230.0
f = 50.0
Idc = 2.0
C = 1000e-6
Vm = Vrms*math.sqrt(2)
Vr = Idc/(2*f*C)
Vdc = Vm - Vr/2
print(round(Vm,2))
print(round(Vr,2))
print(round(Vdc,2))

traps: Using 2f in the ripple formula for a half-wave rectifier. Half wave uses f, full wave uses 2f.
Expecting the capacitor to lower the peak inverse voltage. For full-wave circuits the PIV stays the same (Vm bridge, 2Vm centre-tap). For a half-wave circuit the capacitor doubles it, from Vm to 2Vm.
Keeping the unsmoothed average (0.637 Vm for full wave) as Vdc. With a capacitor, Vdc climbs towards Vm.
Treating a bigger capacitor as free improvement. It narrows the conduction angle and raises the repetitive peak diode current and supply current distortion.
Swapping the load preferences: the C filter suits light loads, the series L filter suits heavy loads.

quiz.q: State the ripple formula for a full-wave rectifier with a capacitor filter and name every symbol.
quiz.a: Vr = Idc/(2fC); Idc is load DC current in A, f supply frequency in Hz, C capacitance in F.

quiz.q: Why does a capacitor filter suit light loads better than heavy loads?
quiz.a: Vr is proportional to Idc, so ripple rises with load current; holding the same ripple at high current needs a much larger, costlier capacitor.

quiz.q: A half-wave rectifier with C = 470 µF runs at 50 Hz and delivers Idc = 0.5 A. Find the ripple.
In the worked example the capacitor is doubled to 2000 µF. Find the new ripple and Vdc.
Increasing C raises Vdc only slightly but raises the diode peak current a lot. Explain.
quiz.a: The charge the load takes in each ripple cycle, Idc/(2f) for full wave, is fixed by the load. A larger C holds the voltage up longer, so the diode conducts for a shorter angle and the same charge flows in a narrower, taller pulse. Vdc saturates near Vm because it can never exceed the peak.

quiz.q: An LC filter designed for full load shows an output rising towards Vm at no load. Why, and what fixes it?
quiz.a: At no load the inductor has almost no current to store energy in, so its filtering action disappears; the capacitor charges to the peak and has no discharge path. A bleeder resistor drawing a minimum current restores the inductor action.

beyond: Not for the exam. In a real DC link the capacitor is chosen by its ripple current rating, not only by capacitance, because the narrow pulses heat it. Electrolytic banks age, so a dried capacitor raising ripple until a downstream converter trips is a common field failure. Modern designs shrink the bank with active ripple compensation or a PFC front end (see 2.8).
